h1:
A Full Day at the Ancient City
Cycling Past Replica Temples and Palaces
intro: The Ancient City (Muang Boran) in Samut Prakan is an open-air museum spread across more than 800 rai, laid out in the shape of a shrunken map of Thailand. It's too big to cover on foot, so the most fun and best-value way to see it is to rent a bike and ride from the north of the map down to the south in a single day. This is a full-day cycling plan that orders the route so you never have to double back, with rest stops for food and the highlights you shouldn't skip.
chips: 🚲 Rent a bike for the whole day
🏯 Replica temples and palaces from across Thailand

blocks.html: If you've heard the Ancient City is "too big to walk," that's true. The grounds cover more than 800 rai, designed to mirror the shape of Thailand's map, with temples, palaces, stupas, and old markets from every region brought together in one place. On foot, you'd see less than half in a single day. Most people who've been say renting a bike is the way to go — you cruise along with a cool breeze and can pull over to take photos anywhere you want to stop.

This plan follows the shape of the Thailand map, starting in the northern zone (the top of the map) and working down through the northeast, central, and finishing in the south near the exit, so you never have to loop back. It's ideal if you want to catch all the highlights without wearing yourself out.

blocks.text: Before you go — entry fees, hours, and getting there

items: Opening hours — daily 9:00 AM–7:00 PM, last tickets at 6:00 PM (aim to enter before 10:00 AM so you have a full day to ride)
Entry for Thai nationals — adults 400 THB, children 6–14 years 250 THB
Standard bike rental — available at the entrance from 9:00 AM (regular bikes are sometimes free during promotions — check at the service point first)
Electric bike — around 100 THB for 1 hour / 250 THB for 3 hours, good if you'd rather not pedal much
Other options — a tram or tuk-tuk tour around the grounds (about 1 hr 30 min per loop), or you can drive your own car in for an extra vehicle entry fee
Getting there — take the BTS Green Line to Kheha station, Exit 3, then a songthaew (route 36) for about 3.8 km. On Saturdays and Sundays there's a free shuttle between BTS Kheha and the Ancient City

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Weekdays are much quieter — easier riding and clear shots for photos — but some food stalls in the floating market may not all be open. If you want a lively market atmosphere, go on a Saturday or Sunday. Bring water and a hat either way, since the midday sun is strong and shade only comes in patches.

blocks.text: Full-day cycling plan — start north, finish south

items.activity: Arrive at the Ancient City, buy tickets and rent a bike at the service point out front
items.note: Grab the paper map at the rental point — it makes planning your route much easier

items.activity: Ride into the northern zone, stopping at Lanna-style wooden temples and viharns
items.note: The morning sun is still gentle — a good time to photograph the wooden viharns

items.activity: Stop at Mount Sumeru and the lakeside pavilion for water-reflection photos
items.note: This stretch is shady and easy riding — a good spot to pull over for a drink

items.activity: Ride to the old floating market, park the bike, and wander for something to eat
items.note: This is the main food spot in the city — noodles, curry-over-rice, and Thai sweets

items.activity: Have lunch at a stall in the floating market, and try old-style Thai sweets with herbal drinks
items.note: Prices are more reasonable than you'd expect — single-plate dishes start in the tens of baht

items.activity: Stroll past the Thai houses and old homes around the market, cooling off before riding on
items.note: Early afternoon is the hottest — resting in the shade a while beats pushing through the heat

items.activity: Ride into the northeastern zone to see the replica Khmer stone sanctuaries
items.note: The stone-sanctuary angles photograph well in the afternoon — the low light brings out the texture of the stone

items.activity: Enter the central zone for the replica Sanphet Prasat and Dusit Maha Prasat throne halls
items.note: An architectural highlight that many say is the most impressive in the whole place

items.activity: Stop at the Arahant pavilion and the cluster of stupas in the center, taking photos before the evening light
items.note: The crowds start thinning here — easy riding and clear shots

blocks.label: Evening
blocks.title: Southern region — wrap up the trip

items.activity: Ride down into the southern zone for southern-style architecture and a replica mosque
items.note: It's near the exit — saving this zone for last means no backtracking

items.activity: Ride back to return the bike at the entrance, stopping by the souvenir shop
items.note: Return the bike before 6:00 PM to leave time for the trip home

items.activity: Leave the Ancient City and catch a ride back to BTS Kheha
items.note: If you've still got energy, the Erawan Museum or a crocodile farm are nearby along the same route

items.name: Sanphet Prasat Throne Hall
items.blurb: A replica throne hall with an Ayutthaya-style spired roof and gilded carved woodwork — the most photographed spot in the city.

items.name: Old floating market
items.blurb: The main spot for food and a stroll in the center, with wooden waterside houses serving old-style Thai dishes and sweets.

items.name: Mount Sumeru
items.blurb: A replica mound of Mount Sumeru from the Traiphum cosmology, ringed by pavilions and a pond with a lovely water-reflection angle.

items.name: Replica Khmer stone sanctuaries
items.blurb: A cluster of southern-Isan-style stone sanctuaries with great atmosphere — like Phimai brought close to Bangkok.

blocks.text: What to eat at the Ancient City

blocks.html: The main place to eat is the old floating market in the center, with several stalls for single-plate Thai dishes, noodles, curry-over-rice, and old-style Thai sweets. The atmosphere is wooden houses over the water, and prices are more reasonable than many expect. There are also cafes and drink stands scattered across the various zones, though not densely. Have your main meal at the floating market and keep some snacks and water on you while you ride.

blocks.title: Ride for fun, not to exhaustion
blocks.html: The grounds are huge — don't try to ride the whole thing in one push. Break it into rest stops along the plan. If a standard bike feels too heavy under the strong afternoon sun, switch to an electric bike or hop on the tram for the more distant zones. No need to tough it out.

faq.q: How many hours do you need at the Ancient City to make it worthwhile?
faq.a: To see the highlights from every region, plan for at least 5–6 hours. The grounds cover more than 800 rai, and cycling lets you see far more than walking. Arriving in the morning and leaving in the evening gives you the most relaxed visit.

faq.q: How much does bike rental cost at the Ancient City?
faq.a: Bikes are available to rent at the service point out front, from 9:00 AM. Electric bikes run about 100 THB for 1 hour or 250 THB for 3 hours. It's worth checking the current prices and promotions at the service point before you rent.

faq.q: Can you visit the Ancient City without a car?
faq.a: Yes. Take the BTS Green Line to Kheha station, Exit 3, then a songthaew (route 36) for about 3.8 km. On Saturdays and Sundays there's a free shuttle between BTS Kheha and the Ancient City.

faq.q: What's the Ancient City entry fee for Thai nationals?
faq.a: Adults 400 THB, children aged 6–14 years 250 THB. These are the rates for Thai nationals; foreign visitors pay more. Check the ticket conditions on the website or at the ticket booth before you go.

faq.q: Is it better to visit the Ancient City on a weekday or a weekend?
faq.a: Weekdays are quieter — easier riding and clear photos — but some floating-market stalls may not all be open. If you want a lively market atmosphere and the free shuttle from the BTS, go on a Saturday or Sunday.
